D12 relates the observed food webs of each visit to the number of large
dams between the site and the sea. The webs are reconstructed from the fish
caught, so they are noisy: most of the variation of trophic length is from
one visit to the next at the same site. Here, food webs are instead
predicted from models of the presence of each species, in three steps:

1. Fit a presence model for each species, with the dams and the position
   along the river.
2. Check that the webs generated from these models reproduce the observed
   ones.
3. Generate webs with and without the dams, and measure the dam impact on
   their structure.

The uncertainty of the presence models is carried through to the webs and
the dam impacts by working with joint posterior draws. Food webs are built
at the species level throughout.

## Summary

- presence models of 48 species (99.7% of the fish caught), with the dams
  and the position along the river, generate food webs that reproduce the
  observed ones (calibrated, correlation 0.7-0.9 per visit)
- the species lost with dams are enough to shorten food chains slightly
  and raise diet overlap slightly, at species level
- the dam effects on the observed webs match those on the generated webs:
  dams change food web structure through which species are present, with
  no sign of a further effect
- the dam effect on trophic length is clearer at the species level than with
  size classes, because it comes from the change of top predator (eel, pike,
  salmon replaced by brown trout)
- the number of dams fits as well as any weighting of the dams by rank
- a few dams, first from the sea on large rivers, would bring back most of
  the species if removed; predicted over the whole network, a dam matters
  through the river length it cuts off and its rank from the sea
- this ranking is close to the diadromous connectivity index (river length
  reachable from the sea) with a dam passability of about 0.75

## To do

- Test fragmentation beyond the dams downstream: add the length of the free
  segment holding each site to the presence models; if it matters, the dam
  ranking needs a potamodromous (DCI_p-like) part
- Fix the Roanne-Digoin canal lock: the network routes the upper Loire through it
- Predictive scores of the generated webs across dam weightings (needs the
  presence models refitted for each weighting)

## Setup

```{r setup}
library(renv)
renv::load()
library(targets)
library(here)
tar_config_set(
  store = here::here("_targets")
)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
devtools::load_all()
nice_theme()
```

## Visits

All visits of river (ASPE) sites with fish records, as in D12 (target
`dam_visit`): dams are the large dams and weirs (ROE, drop height
$\geq$ 5 m) between the site and the sea, placed on the AMOBIO network
after a manual review (see D12).

```{r visits}
visit <- tar_read(dam_visit)
settings <- tar_read(dam_web_settings)
c(
  visits = nrow(visit), sites = n_distinct(visit$sandre_code),
  catchments = n_distinct(visit$catchment), with_dam = mean(visit$dams > 0)
)
```

## Presence models

One model per species found at >= `r settings$min_sites` sites (target
`dam_presence_sample`). For visit $i$ at site $s$, in year $t$ and
catchment $c$, the presence $Y_i$ of the species is

$$
\begin{aligned}
Y_i &\sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(p_i), \\
\mathrm{logit}\, p_i &= \beta_0 + \beta_D \log(1 + D_i) + \beta_W W_i
+ \beta_H H_i + \beta_{H^2} H_i^2 + \beta_M M_i \\
&\quad + \alpha_{\mathrm{district}(i)} + \gamma_{\mathrm{protocol}(i)}
+ \beta_A \log A_i + u_s + v_t + w_c
\end{aligned}
$$

with $D_i$ the number of large dams and weirs between the site and the sea,
$W_i$ the log river width, $H_i$ the log altitude and $M_i$ the log
distance to the mouth (centred; see D12 for the choice of these controls),
$A_i$ the fished surface, and iid random effects of the site ($u_s$), the
year ($v_t$) and the catchment ($w_c$). From each model,
`r settings$n_draws` joint draws of the posterior are kept: the linear
predictor of each visit (which includes the random effects) and the dam
effect $\beta_D$, from the same draws.

```{r presence-species}
presence <- tar_read(river_presence)
presence_species <- tar_read(dam_presence_species)
c(
  species = length(presence_species),
  share_of_occurrences = mean(
    presence$species_valid[presence$operation_id %in% visit$operation_id] %in% presence_species
  )
)
```

Dam effect $\beta_D$ per species (posterior mean and 95% credible
interval).

```{r presence-effect-plot}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 10

tar_read(dam_presence_effect) |>
  mutate(
    species = reorder(species, -mean),
    credible = if_else(upper < 0 | lower > 0, "credible", "not credible")
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(mean, species, color = credible)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper), size = 0.3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(credible = "black", `not credible` = "grey60")) +
  labs(x = "Effect of log(1 + large dams downstream)", y = NULL, color = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(face = "italic"))
```

**Results:** the `r length(presence_species)` modelled species cover
almost all the fish caught. About half of them are credibly less frequent
with more dams downstream: the migratory species (sea lamprey, eel,
salmon) and species of large lowland rivers, native or not. As in D12,
brown trout is more frequent with dams; so is the ide, a rare species with
an uncertain effect.

## Species-level food webs

The food web of a set of species is cut out of the species-level metaweb
(target `species_metaweb`): two species are linked if any size class of
the predator eats any size class of the prey. The 10 resources (detritus,
biofilm, macrophytes, phytoplankton, zooplankton, worms, molluscs,
crustaceans, insects, echinoderms) are in every web. Four measures:

- fish richness $S$, the number of fish species;
- trophic length $L$, the maximum prey-averaged trophic level;
- piscivore presence $P$, whether a fish species eats another fish;
- diet overlap $O$, the mean Jaccard similarity of the prey of pairs of
  fish species.

The observed species-level webs are built from the species caught, keeping
only the modelled species (target `dam_web_observed`), so that observed
and generated webs are comparable. They differ from the size-class webs of
D11 and D12, which only keep the size classes caught.

```{r observed-webs}
observed <- tar_read(dam_web_observed)
size_class <- tar_read(foodweb_structure) |>
  filter(survey == "river") |>
  distinct(operation_id, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  mutate(operation_id = as.character(operation_id)) |>
  select(operation_id, trophic_length, fish_diet_overlap)
observed |>
  mutate(operation_id = as.character(operation_id)) |>
  inner_join(size_class, by = "operation_id", suffix = c("", "_size_class")) |>
  summarise(
    trophic_length = cor(trophic_length, trophic_length_size_class, use = "complete"),
    fish_diet_overlap = cor(fish_diet_overlap, fish_diet_overlap_size_class, use = "complete")
  )
```

## Do the presence models reproduce the observed webs?

For each visit and posterior draw, the presence of each species is drawn
from its presence probability, the web of the species present is built,
and its structure measured (target `dam_web_simulated`). Each visit thus
has `r settings$n_draws` generated webs, whose spread carries the
uncertainty of the presence models and the chance of which species are
caught.

```{r generated-webs}
simulated <- tar_read(dam_web_simulated)
metric_label <- c(
  richness = "S: fish richness", trophic_length = "L: trophic length",
  piscivore = "P: piscivore present", fish_diet_overlap = "O: diet overlap (fish)"
)
generated <- lapply(names(metric_label), function(m) {
  web <- simulated$web[, , m, "dams"]
  tibble(
    operation_id = simulated$operation_id, metric = m,
    mean = rowMeans(web, na.rm = TRUE),
    q05 = apply(web, 1, quantile, 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
    q25 = apply(web, 1, quantile, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    q75 = apply(web, 1, quantile, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    q95 = apply(web, 1, quantile, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
}) |>
  bind_rows() |>
  inner_join(
    observed |> tidyr::pivot_longer(-operation_id, names_to = "metric", values_to = "observed"),
    by = c("operation_id", "metric")
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(observed), !is.na(mean)) |>
  left_join(distinct(visit, operation_id, sandre_code), by = "operation_id")
```

Observed against generated structure (mean of the generated webs), one
point per visit; dashed line: 1:1.

```{r generated-observed-plot}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 3.5

generated |>
  filter(metric != "piscivore") |>
  mutate(metric = factor(metric, names(metric_label), metric_label)) |>
  ggplot(aes(mean, observed)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.4, alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", color = "#B2182B") +
  facet_wrap(~metric, nrow = 1, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "Generated (mean over draws)", y = "Observed")
```

Agreement between observed and generated structure: correlation per visit
and per site (means over the visits of a site), and share of the visits
whose observed value falls within the central 50% and 90% of the
generated webs (expected: 0.5 and 0.9 if the generated webs are
calibrated).

```{r generated-observed-table}
generated |>
  summarise(
    correlation_visit = cor(mean, observed),
    coverage_50 = mean(observed >= q25 & observed <= q75),
    coverage_90 = mean(observed >= q05 & observed <= q95),
    .by = metric
  ) |>
  left_join(
    generated |>
      summarise(mean = mean(mean), observed = mean(observed), .by = c(metric, sandre_code)) |>
      summarise(correlation_site = cor(mean, observed), .by = metric),
    by = "metric"
  ) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

The species are drawn independently of each other, given their presence
probabilities. Co-occurrence of each pair of species: observed number of
visits where both are caught against the number expected from the
presence probabilities (pairs expected at >= 20 visits).

```{r cooccurrence-plot}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5

probability <- tar_read(dam_presence_probability)
caught <- sapply(
  colnames(probability),
  \(s) as.numeric(rownames(probability) %in% presence$operation_id[presence$species_valid == s])
)
pair <- upper.tri(diag(ncol(probability)))
cooccurrence <- tibble(
  observed = (t(caught) %*% caught)[pair],
  expected = (t(probability) %*% probability)[pair]
) |>
  filter(expected >= 20)
cooccurrence |>
  ggplot(aes(expected, observed)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8, alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", color = "#B2182B") +
  scale_x_continuous(transform = "log1p") +
  scale_y_continuous(transform = "log1p") +
  labs(x = "Expected co-occurrences (independent species)", y = "Observed co-occurrences")
```

**Results:** the generated webs reproduce the observed ones well. Fish
richness, trophic length and diet overlap of the generated webs follow the
observed values closely, visit by visit and even more site by site, and
they are calibrated: the observed value falls within the central 50% and
90% of the generated webs about as often as expected. Piscivore presence
is the exception, but only because almost every web has a piscivore, so
there is little to predict. Species pairs co-occur about as often as
expected from independent presences, with some exceptions: a few species
cluster more than predicted (spined loach with lowland species), and some
upland and lowland species are predicted to co-occur at a few sites where
they are never caught together.

*To discuss: the species-level webs keep all the size classes of each
species, so they differ from the size-class webs of D11 and D12
(correlation about 0.7-0.75 for trophic length and diet overlap).*

## Dam impacts on the generated webs

### Webs without dams

Each visit's webs are generated a second time with the dam term of every
presence model set to 0, with the same posterior draws and the same random
numbers (target `dam_web_counterfactual`). The difference between the two
sets of webs is the change in structure due to the species that the dams
remove or add. For each posterior draw, the differences are averaged over
the visits with at least one dam, overall and by number of dams; the spread
over the draws gives the uncertainty.

```{r counterfactual}
counterfactual <- tar_read(dam_web_counterfactual) |>
  summarise(
    mean = mean(difference, na.rm = TRUE),
    lower = quantile(difference, 0.025, na.rm = TRUE),
    upper = quantile(difference, 0.975, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = c(dam_class, metric)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    metric = factor(metric, names(metric_label), metric_label),
    dam_class = factor(dam_class, c("1", "2-3", "4+", "all"), c("1 dam", "2-3 dams", "4+ dams", "all dammed visits"))
  )
```

Change in the structure of the generated webs, observed dams minus no dam,
at the visits with dams (posterior mean and 95% credible interval).

```{r counterfactual-plot}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 3.5

counterfactual |>
  ggplot(aes(mean, dam_class)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper), size = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~metric, nrow = 1, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev) +
  labs(x = "Observed dams - no dam", y = NULL)
```

**Results:** the species that the dams remove are enough to change the
webs. At the visits with dams, the generated webs without dams have about
one more fish species, slightly longer food chains and slightly less diet
overlap between fish species. These changes grow with the number of dams.
Piscivore presence does not change: almost every web keeps a piscivore.
The changes are small compared with the differences between visits.

### Dam effect fitted to generated and observed webs

The D12 models of web structure on log(1 + dams) (fish richness, Poisson;
trophic length of the webs with a piscivore and diet overlap, Gaussian;
same controls and random effects as the presence models; visits with at
least 3 fish species) are fitted to the observed species-level webs and to
`r length(tar_read(dam_realisation))` realisations of the generated webs,
each from one posterior draw of the presence models (targets
`dam_structure_observed` and `dam_structure_generated`). Each realisation
uses the same parameter values at every visit, so it keeps the uncertainty
of the presence models that is shared across visits (e.g. the dam effect
of the eel). The posterior draws of the dam effect are pooled over the
realisations: their spread combines the uncertainty of the presence models
and of the structure model.

```{r structure-dam}
structure_label <- metric_label[c("richness", "trophic_length", "fish_diet_overlap")]
structure_dam <- bind_rows(
  generated = tar_read(dam_structure_generated),
  observed = tar_read(dam_structure_observed),
  .id = "webs"
) |>
  mutate(response = factor(response, names(structure_label), structure_label))
structure_dam |>
  summarise(
    mean = mean(draw), lower = quantile(draw, 0.025), upper = quantile(draw, 0.975),
    .by = c(webs, response)
  ) |>
  arrange(response, webs) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

Posterior of the dam effect fitted to the observed webs and to the
generated webs (pooled over realisations).

```{r structure-dam-plot}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 3.5

structure_dam |>
  ggplot(aes(draw, fill = webs, color = webs)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~response, nrow = 1, scales = "free") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(observed = "grey30", generated = "#B2182B")) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(observed = "grey30", generated = "#B2182B")) +
  labs(x = "Effect of log(1 + large dams downstream)", y = "Posterior density", fill = NULL, color = NULL)
```

**Results:** fitted to the generated webs, the model gives about the same
dam effects as fitted to the observed webs: fewer species, slightly
shorter chains and slightly more diet overlap with more dams, all
credible, with similar sizes. Since the generated webs change with the
dams only through which species are present, the dam effects on the
observed webs are what the loss of species predicts: there is no sign of
a further effect of the dams on web structure. Pooling over realisations
matters: the uncertainty of the presence models is about as large as that
of the structure model.

*To discuss: the change from removing all dams (above) is larger than the
fitted dam effect per unit of log(1 + dams); the structure model controls
for the position and has site random effects, which may absorb part of
the difference between dammed and undammed sites. The two quantities are
not the same, and the comparison with the observed webs is made with the
fitted model.*

## Species-level and size-class webs

The dam effects on the observed webs are clearer at the species level
than with the size-class webs of D11 and D12. Same model, same visits,
fitted to the species-level and to the size-class metrics (fish richness
is the same in both; targets `dam_structure_observed` and
`dam_structure_size_class`).

```{r aggregation-effect}
bind_rows(
  `species level` = tar_read(dam_structure_observed),
  `size classes` = tar_read(dam_structure_size_class),
  .id = "webs"
) |>
  summarise(
    mean = mean(draw), lower = quantile(draw, 0.025), upper = quantile(draw, 0.975),
    .by = c(response, webs)
  ) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

Species holding the highest trophic level of each web, by number of dams
downstream (share of the visits; species at the top of at least 5% of the
webs of a class), and mean trophic length of the webs topped by each
species, at both levels (target `top_trophic_species`).

```{r top-species}
top <- tar_read(top_trophic_species) |>
  left_join(select(visit, operation_id, dams), by = "operation_id") |>
  mutate(dam_class = cut(dams, c(-Inf, 0, 1, 3, Inf), c("0", "1", "2-3", "4+")))
top |>
  count(dam_class, top_species) |>
  mutate(share = round(n / sum(n), 2), .by = dam_class) |>
  filter(max(share) >= 0.05, .by = top_species) |>
  select(-n) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = dam_class, values_from = share, values_fill = 0)
top |>
  summarise(
    webs = n(),
    trophic_length_species = round(mean(trophic_length_species), 2),
    trophic_length_size_class = round(mean(trophic_length_size_class), 2),
    .by = top_species
  ) |>
  filter(webs >= 100) |>
  arrange(desc(webs))
```

**Results:** fish richness responds the same at both levels, and diet
overlap almost the same (only less precisely with size classes). Trophic
length differs: its dam effect is about twice as strong at the species
level. The reason is the change of top predator: with more dams, the eel,
the pike and the salmon give way to brown trout at the top of the webs. At
the species level, each species carries the diet of all its size classes,
so pike or pikeperch sit well above brown trout. In the size-class webs,
they only reach their high trophic level when large individuals are
caught, so the gap with brown trout is about half as large, and so is the
dam effect. Species-level trophic length measures which species are
present; size-class trophic length also depends on the sizes caught.

## Dam weighting

Does every dam count the same? The $k$-th dam between the site and the sea
is weighted by $w^{k-1}$: $w = 1$ gives the number of dams (used above),
$w = 0$ only the first dam, $0 < w < 1$ a saturating count and $w > 1$ an
accelerating one; $\log(1 + \text{weighted dams})$ replaces
$\log(1 + D_i)$. The models of the observed species-level structure
(target `dam_weight_structure`) and the presence models of the 48 species
(coarser grid of $w$; target `dam_weight_presence`) are refitted for each
$w$ and compared by their log marginal likelihood. WAIC is not used here:
it is unstable for the rare species (differences of thousands between
neighbouring weights).

```{r dam-weight}
weight_structure <- tar_read(dam_weight_structure) |>
  mutate(delta = mlik - mlik[weight == 1], .by = response) |>
  mutate(panel = metric_label[response])
weight_presence <- tar_read(dam_weight_presence) |>
  mutate(delta = mlik - mlik[weight == 1], .by = species)
weight_presence |>
  slice_max(mlik, n = 1, by = species) |>
  count(best_weight = weight, name = "species")
```

Log marginal likelihood of each weighting relative to the number of dams
($w = 1$): web structure (observed species-level webs) and the presence
models summed over the 48 species (grey band: within 2).

```{r dam-weight-plot}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 3.5

bind_rows(
  weight_structure |> select(panel, weight, delta),
  weight_presence |>
    summarise(delta = sum(delta), .by = weight) |>
    mutate(panel = "Presence, sum over species")
) |>
  mutate(panel = factor(panel, c(metric_label[c("richness", "trophic_length", "fish_diet_overlap")], "Presence, sum over species"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(weight, delta)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = -2, ymax = 2, fill = "grey90") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey60") +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~panel, nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Rank weight w (0: first dam only, 1: number of dams)", y = "Log marginal likelihood\n- number of dams")
```

Species whose presence model fits clearly better (by more than 2) with
another weighting than the number of dams.

```{r dam-weight-species}
weight_presence |>
  slice_max(mlik, n = 1, by = species) |>
  filter(delta > 2) |>
  transmute(species, best_weight = weight, delta = round(delta, 1)) |>
  arrange(desc(delta))
```

**Results:** counting every dam the same fits as well as any other
weighting. For fish richness, the number of dams fits best, and counting
only the first dam fits clearly worse. For trophic length and diet
overlap, all weightings fit about equally: the data cannot tell how the
dams add up for the web structure. Summed over the 48 species, a
saturating count (the first dams matter more) fits slightly better than the
number of dams, and an accelerating count clearly worse; most species show
no clear preference. The eel needs the number of dams: counting only the
first dam, or making later dams weigh more, fits clearly worse. A few
lowland species (white bream, minnow, sunbleak, pikeperch, wels catfish,
*Leuciscus burdigalensis*) fit better with the first dam only.

## Dam removal

How much would removing each dam change the species and the webs
upstream? Removing any one of the dams downstream of a site lowers its
number of dams by one, so the webs of each visit are generated once more
with one dam fewer, with the same draws and random numbers (target
`dam_web_one_less`). The importance of a dam is the change at the sampled
sites upstream of it (mean over the visits of each site), summed over
these sites, for each posterior draw (target `dam_removal`). The gain in
fish richness of a dam is thus the expected number of species found in
addition, summed over the sites upstream.

```{r dam-removal}
removal <- tar_read(dam_removal)
dam_info <- tar_read(large_dam) |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(roe_code, name, river, kind, drop_height_min, altitude)
dams_below <- tar_read(dam_dam) |>
  filter(position == "upstream") |>
  count(roe_code = operation_id, name = "dams_below")
importance <- removal$web |>
  summarise(
    sites = first(sites),
    lower = quantile(total, 0.025), upper = quantile(total, 0.975),
    total = mean(total), per_site = mean(per_site),
    .by = c(roe_code, metric)
  ) |>
  left_join(dam_info, by = "roe_code") |>
  left_join(dams_below, by = "roe_code") |>
  mutate(
    rank = coalesce(dams_below, 0L) + 1,
    rank_class = cut(rank, c(0, 1, 2, 4, Inf), c("1st", "2nd", "3rd-4th", "5th+"))
  )
richness_gain <- filter(importance, metric == "richness")
c(
  dams = nrow(richness_gain),
  credible_gain = sum(richness_gain$lower > 0),
  share_top_20 = sum(sort(richness_gain$total, decreasing = TRUE)[1:20]) / sum(richness_gain$total)
)
```

The 15 dams whose removal would add the most fish species (summed over the
sites upstream, posterior mean and 95% credible interval), with the change
in trophic length summed over the same sites.

```{r dam-removal-table}
richness_gain |>
  arrange(desc(total)) |>
  head(15) |>
  left_join(
    importance |> filter(metric == "trophic_length") |> select(roe_code, trophic_length = total),
    by = "roe_code"
  ) |>
  transmute(
    roe_code, name = stringr::str_trunc(name, 30), river = stringr::str_trunc(river, 22),
    kind, height = paste0(">= ", drop_height_min, " m"), rank, sites,
    richness = sprintf("%.1f (%.1f, %.1f)", total, lower, upper),
    trophic_length = round(trophic_length, 2)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Richness gain of each dam against the number of sampled sites upstream
(left) and per site against its rank from the sea (right).

```{r dam-removal-plot}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4

patchwork::wrap_plots(
  richness_gain |>
    ggplot(aes(sites, total, color = rank_class)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
    scale_x_log10() +
    scale_color_viridis_d(end = 0.9) +
    labs(x = "Sampled sites upstream", y = "Species gained,\nsummed over the sites", color = "Rank from\nthe sea"),
  richness_gain |>
    ggplot(aes(rank_class, per_site)) +
    geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.8) +
    labs(x = "Rank from the sea", y = "Species gained per site")
)
```

Species that would gain the most (expected number of sites upstream where
each is found in addition, summed over the removals of single dams).

```{r dam-removal-species}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5

removal$species |>
  summarise(sites_gained = sum(sites_gained), .by = species) |>
  filter(abs(sites_gained) >= 5) |>
  mutate(species = reorder(species, sites_gained)) |>
  ggplot(aes(sites_gained, species)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Sites gained, summed over single-dam removals", y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(face = "italic"))
```

**Results:** most dams matter little for the sampled sites: about a fifth
of the `r nrow(richness_gain)` dams with sites upstream would credibly add
species if removed, and 20 dams account for most of the total gain. The
most important dams are those with many sampled sites upstream and few
other dams downstream: the first dam from the sea on large rivers, such as
the weir of Vichy on the Allier, Châtellerault on the Vienne or the
Abattoir weir on the Cher. Per site, the gain falls quickly with the rank
of the dam from the sea; this follows partly from the model itself, in
which a dam adds less where there are already many. The species that would
gain most are the eel, the salmon and lowland species (topmouth gudgeon,
chub, gudgeon, bitterling, white bream); brown trout would lose sites.

*To discuss: the second most important dam is a lock of the Roanne-Digoin
canal, with 66 sites upstream: the network may route the upper Loire
through the canal, which would be a topology artefact to check (as for the
canal of restitution "GHE"). Importance is measured at sampled sites only,
so it depends on where sampling took place, not on the length of river
upstream.*

### Dam importance over the river network

The importance above depends on where sampling took place. Here, presence
is predicted on every reach of the river network instead (RHT reaches of
the four districts, placed on the AMOBIO network by their midpoint, within
the range of width, altitude and distance to the mouth of the visits;
target `network_reach`), for a typical site and year (reference protocol,
median fished surface), with the observed number of dams downstream and
with one dam fewer. The dam weighting is averaged over the rank weights
(Bayesian model averaging): each species is refitted for each weight
(target `dam_presence_weight_sample`), and each posterior draw comes from
one weight, drawn with probabilities from the log marginal likelihoods.
The importance of a dam is the change in presence summed over the species
and over the reaches upstream, weighted by their length: species x km
gained (target `dam_removal_network`).

```{r network-removal}
network <- tar_read(dam_removal_network)
traits <- tar_read(dam_traits)
network_gain <- network$richness |>
  summarise(
    lower = quantile(gain, 0.025), upper = quantile(gain, 0.975), gain = mean(gain),
    .by = roe_code
  ) |>
  left_join(network$upstream_km, by = "roe_code") |>
  mutate(per_km = gain / km) |>
  left_join(traits, by = "roe_code")
c(
  reaches = nrow(tar_read(network_reach)), dams = nrow(network_gain),
  credible_gain = sum(network_gain$lower > 0),
  share_top_20 = sum(sort(network_gain$gain, decreasing = TRUE)[1:20]) / sum(network_gain$gain)
)
network$model_weight |>
  summarise(mean_probability = round(mean(probability), 2), .by = weight)
```

The 15 dams whose removal would add the most species x km (posterior mean
and 95% credible interval), with the river length upstream and the gain per
km.

```{r network-removal-table}
network_gain |>
  arrange(desc(gain)) |>
  head(15) |>
  transmute(
    roe_code, name = stringr::str_trunc(name, 30), river = stringr::str_trunc(river, 22),
    kind, rank, dist_mouth_km = round(dist_mouth_km), upstream_km = round(km),
    gain = sprintf("%.0f (%.0f, %.0f)", gain, lower, upper), per_km = round(per_km, 2)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

### What do the most important dams have in common?

Spearman correlation of the total gain and of the gain per km of river
upstream with the position and characteristics of the dams (target
`dam_traits`): river length upstream (within the range of the visits),
share of the river length of its catchment upstream of the dam, drained
area and Strahler order at the dam, rank from the sea, number of large dams
upstream, distance to the mouth, altitude and drop height class.

```{r dam-traits-correlation}
network_gain |>
  transmute(
    gain, per_km, upstream_km = km, upstream_share, drained_area, strahler,
    rank, dams_upstream, dist_mouth_km, altitude, height = drop_height_min
  ) |>
  cor(method = "spearman", use = "pairwise") |>
  (\(x) x[c("gain", "per_km"), -(1:2)])() |>
  round(2)
```

Total gain against the river length upstream (left) and gain per km
against the rank from the sea (middle) and the altitude of the dam
(right).

```{r dam-traits-plot}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4

network_gain <- network_gain |>
  mutate(rank_class = cut(rank, c(0, 1, 2, 4, Inf), c("1st", "2nd", "3rd-4th", "5th+")))
patchwork::wrap_plots(
  ggplot(network_gain, aes(km, gain, color = rank_class)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
    scale_x_log10() +
    scale_y_log10() +
    scale_color_viridis_d(end = 0.9) +
    labs(x = "River upstream (km)", y = "Species x km gained", color = "Rank from\nthe sea"),
  ggplot(network_gain, aes(rank_class, per_km)) +
    geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.8) +
    labs(x = "Rank from the sea", y = "Species gained per km"),
  ggplot(network_gain, aes(altitude, per_km, color = rank_class)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
    scale_x_log10() +
    scale_color_viridis_d(end = 0.9, guide = "none") +
    labs(x = "Altitude of the dam (m)", y = "Species gained per km"),
  widths = c(1.2, 1, 1)
)
```

**Results:** predicted over the whole network, the ranking is close to the
one from the sampled sites, but it covers more dams and no longer depends
on where sampling took place. Removing almost any dam would credibly bring
back some species upstream, but a few dams dominate: 20 dams account for
more than half of the total gain. They are the first dams from the sea on
large rivers: the weir of Vichy on the Allier, Châtellerault on the
Vienne, the Abattoir weir on the Cher, Le Temple on the Lot, Saint
Fraimbault on the Mayenne. Two things make a dam important. First, how
much river it cuts off: the total gain follows the river length upstream,
the drained area and the share of its catchment above it. Second, how
many dams already stand downstream: the gain per km of river falls
steeply with the rank of the dam from the sea, and it is also larger for
dams at low altitude, where the reaches upstream hold more of the species
that dams remove. The drop height plays almost no role. The averaging gives
slightly more weight to the weightings in which the first dams count most,
so the data do not contradict this rank effect, but it remains largely set
by the shape of the model, in which a dam adds less where there are
already many.

*To discuss: a lock of the Roanne-Digoin canal ranks fourth because the
network routes the upper Loire through the canal: it is the only large dam
downstream of Villerest. This adds a dam to every upper-Loire site in all
the analyses (D12 and D13) and needs fixing in the network or in the dam
review. The importance only covers the reaches within the range of the
visits, and assumes that all dams act the same (no effect of height, type
or fish pass in the presence models).*

### Dam importance and river connectivity

The dendritic connectivity index (DCI, Cote et al. 2009, Landscape
Ecology) is the usual way to score river fragmentation. It has two forms,
computed here on the same reaches (target `dam_connectivity`):

- diadromous (DCI_d): the share of river length reachable from the sea. A
  reach with D dams downstream counts its length times p^D, with p the
  passability of a dam, so removing one of the dams adds the length of each
  reach upstream times p^(D-1) (1-p)
- potamodromous (DCI_p): the chance that two points of the river are
  connected. Removing an impassable dam joins the free segment above it to
  the one holding it, adding twice the product of their lengths

Both are usually divided by the river length of the catchment (and its
square for DCI_p), to score each catchment from 0 to 1; both forms are
shown. Spearman correlation of the species x km gained with the gain in
each index, and number of dams in common in the top 20.

```{r connectivity-comparison}
connectivity <- network_gain |>
  select(roe_code, gain, km) |>
  inner_join(tar_read(dam_connectivity), by = "roe_code") |>
  mutate(
    dci_d_0.5_catchment = dci_d_0.5 / catchment_km,
    dci_p_catchment = dci_p / catchment_km^2
  )
index <- c(
  km = "River upstream (km)",
  dci_d_0.25 = "DCI_d, p = 0.25", dci_d_0.5 = "DCI_d, p = 0.5", dci_d_0.75 = "DCI_d, p = 0.75",
  dci_d_0.5_catchment = "DCI_d, p = 0.5, per catchment",
  dci_p = "DCI_p", dci_p_catchment = "DCI_p, per catchment"
)
top_20 <- function(score) connectivity$roe_code[order(score, decreasing = TRUE)[1:20]]
tibble(
  index = index,
  spearman = sapply(names(index), \(v) cor(connectivity$gain, connectivity[[v]], method = "spearman")),
  top_20_shared = sapply(names(index), \(v) length(intersect(top_20(connectivity$gain), top_20(connectivity[[v]]))))
) |>
  mutate(spearman = round(spearman, 2)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Species x km gained against the gain in DCI_d with p = 0.75 (left) and in
DCI_p (right).

```{r connectivity-plot}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4

connectivity <- connectivity |>
  left_join(select(network_gain, roe_code, rank_class), by = "roe_code")
patchwork::wrap_plots(
  ggplot(connectivity, aes(dci_d_0.75, gain, color = rank_class)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
    scale_x_log10() +
    scale_y_log10() +
    scale_color_viridis_d(end = 0.9, guide = "none") +
    labs(x = "DCI_d gain, p = 0.75 (km)", y = "Species x km gained"),
  ggplot(connectivity, aes(dci_p + 1, gain, color = rank_class)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
    scale_x_log10() +
    scale_y_log10() +
    scale_color_viridis_d(end = 0.9) +
    labs(x = "DCI_p gain + 1 (km²)", y = "Species x km gained", color = "Rank from\nthe sea")
)
```

**Results:** the dam ranking is almost the same as the one given by the
diadromous connectivity index with a passability of about 0.75: the two
share 19 of their top 20 dams. This is expected from the form of the
models: the gain of a dam is a sum over the river upstream, weighted by
length, of a change that shrinks with the number of dams already
downstream, which is how the diadromous index is built. The models fix how
fast it shrinks (about as fast as a passability of 0.75) and weight each km
by the species it could hold, but this second part changes the ranking
little. The potamodromous index ranks dams differently, favouring dams
that split two long free segments wherever they stand. Dividing by the
catchment length gives another ranking again, led by small coastal rivers:
it scores the improvement within a catchment, not the absolute gain.

*To discuss: the presence models only count the dams downstream of a site,
so they cannot capture fragmentation away from the sea, which is what the
potamodromous index measures; the weak match with it follows from the
model and is not a finding. Whether fragmentation matters beyond the dams
downstream is the segment-length test in the To do list.*
